title: How to know if you've got product-market fit: a curated set of definitions and signals
summary: Lenny curates the most actionable definitions of product-market fit from founders and investors, split into pre-product and post-product signals. Key tests: retention curves that flatten, the 40% "very disappointed" survey, organic growth, and LTV exceeding CAC. He closes with Ben Horowitz's point that PMF is not a single moment.

principles.text: Most people have only a vague grasp of PMF, and few pursue it systematically. Collect concrete definitions and measure against them.
principles.quote: I’ve noticed that most people (including myself) have only a vague grasp on what product-market fit actually is. And even fewer people are going after it in a systematic way.

principles.text: Before you have a product, test PMF by trying to get people to pay now, even via an invoice for early access.
principles.quote: Nothing will be a better signal of interest and PMF if you can get people to put down money before you have a product.

principles.text: Retention is a core post-product PMF test: if cohort retention curves flatten, a group of customers is finding lasting value.
principles.quote: If it flattens off at some point, you have probably found product/market fit for some market or audience.

principles.text: Survey users on how they'd feel if the product disappeared; more than 40% answering 'very disappointed' signals PMF.
principles.quote: If that percentage is over 40%, you have PMF.

principles.text: Organic, word-of-mouth growth is a key PMF indicator: users who love a product spontaneously tell others.
principles.quote: Organic growth is the key indicator of product/market fit.

principles.text: PMF is not a one-time, discrete point in time; competitors and markets keep evolving, so keep checking.
principles.quote: Product/market fit isn’t a one-time, discrete point in time that announces itself with trumpet fanfares.
